title: Reading the gut wall, oesophagus to colon
summary: One four-layer plan, rebuilt six times for six different jobs — and how to tell them apart in 3D.
objectives: Name the four layers of the gut wall and what each contains
Identify the oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum and colon from their wall alone
Relate each specialisation (glands, folds, villi, lymphoid tissue, taeniae) to the job of that segment
Place the two enteric plexuses and explain what each controls
takeaways: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa or adventitia — the plan never changes, the details do.
Oesophagus: stratified squamous epithelium and an adventitia. Stomach: pits, parietal and chief cells, three muscle layers.
Brunner glands in the submucosa mean duodenum; tall plicae and villi mean jejunum; Peyer patches mean ileum.
The colon has no villi, deep straight crypts packed with goblet cells, and its longitudinal muscle gathered into three taeniae.
Meissner's plexus lies in the submucosa and runs secretion; Auerbach's lies between the muscle coats and runs motility.

steps.title: The oesophagus: built for friction
steps.text:
Every segment of the tube has the same four layers: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal) and an outer serosa or adventitia. Learn to read one and you can read them all.

In the model the oesophagus wears a thick non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium — boluses scrape, they are not digested here. Mucous oesophageal glands sit in the submucosa and send ducts up through the mucosa. The muscle is skeletal in the upper third, smooth in the lower third and mixed between. Outside there is only loose adventitia: the thoracic oesophagus lies in the posterior mediastinum, not in the peritoneal cavity.
steps.clinical: With no serosa to hold sutures and no barrier to spread, oesophageal anastomoses leak more readily and oesophageal cancers reach mediastinal structures early. In Barrett oesophagus the squamous lining of the lower end is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells — a metaplasia driven by acid reflux.

check.q: Why does the thoracic oesophagus have an adventitia rather than a serosa?
check.a: It lies in the posterior mediastinum, outside any serous cavity, so there is no mesothelium to cover it — only loose connective tissue.

steps.title: The stomach: a gland that churns
steps.text:
The gastric mucosa is a sheet of gastric pits lined by surface mucous cells, each pit leading down into tubular glands. In the fundus and body the glands hold parietal (oxyntic) cells in their upper half — acid and intrinsic factor — and chief (zymogen) cells at their base, making pepsinogen. The mucosa and submucosa are thrown into rugae that flatten as the stomach fills.

The muscularis externa has a third, inner oblique layer, found nowhere else in the tube. It is what lets the stomach grind and mix rather than simply propel.
steps.clinical: Autoimmune gastritis targets parietal cells and intrinsic factor, giving an atrophic, achlorhydric body mucosa and B12 deficiency. The antrum, which has mucous glands and G cells rather than parietal cells, is spared.

check.q: Which gastric cell makes intrinsic factor, and what happens when it is lost?
check.a: The parietal cell. Without it vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed in the terminal ileum, and pernicious anaemia with subacute combined degeneration of the cord can follow.

steps.title: The duodenum: neutralising the acid
steps.text:
The first part of the small intestine receives acid chyme from the pylorus. Its signature is in the submucosa: coiled Brunner glands whose ducts pierce the muscularis mucosae and empty an alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus into the crypts. No other segment has glands in the submucosa below the oesophagus.

The villi are broad and leaf-shaped, and there are no tall plicae in the first part. Bile and pancreatic juice enter at the major papilla in the second part, finishing the job of neutralisation.
steps.clinical: Duodenal ulcers are almost all in the first part, where acid arrives before bicarbonate and bile have mixed in. A posterior ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery, which lies directly behind it.

check.q: You see mucous glands in the submucosa of a small bowel section. Where is it from?
check.a: The duodenum — Brunner glands are its identifying feature.

steps.title: The jejunum: surface area
steps.text:
Absorption needs area, and the jejunum multiplies it three times over. Plicae circulares are permanent circular folds with a submucosal core. On them stand villi, finger-like projections with a lamina propria core holding a capillary network and a blind-ended central lacteal that collects absorbed fat as chylomicrons. The enterocytes carry a microvillous brush border.

Between the villi, crypts of Lieberkühn hold the stem cells that renew the epithelium every four to five days, with Paneth cells at their base secreting antimicrobial defensins and lysozyme.
steps.clinical: In coeliac disease the villi flatten and the crypts lengthen (villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia) and intraepithelial lymphocytes increase. The diagnostic biopsy is taken from the distal duodenum, where the change is reliably present.
steps.pitfall: Plicae are not villi. Plicae are visible to the naked eye and do not flatten when the gut is distended; villi are microscopic and sit on top of them.

check.q: What forms the core of a plica circularis, and what forms the core of a villus?
check.a: A plica has a submucosal core; a villus has a core of lamina propria.

steps.title: The ileum: immune surveillance
steps.text:
Distally the villi become shorter, goblet cells more numerous and the plicae fade away. The ileum's hallmark is in the antimesenteric wall: Peyer patches, aggregates of lymphoid follicles with germinal centres that bulge through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa.

The epithelium over each patch includes M cells, which take up antigen from the lumen and hand it to dendritic cells and lymphocytes beneath — the inductive site for gut IgA.
steps.clinical: The terminal ileum is the only site of B12–intrinsic factor and bile-salt absorption, so resection or Crohn disease there causes B12 deficiency and bile-acid diarrhoea. Hypertrophied Peyer patches after a viral illness are a common lead point for ileocolic intussusception in infants.

check.q: Which part of the small intestine has Peyer patches, and on which side of the wall?
check.a: The ileum, on the antimesenteric border.

steps.title: The colon: water and mucus
steps.text:
The colon absorbs water and salt, not nutrients, so the villi are gone. The mucosa is flat with deep, straight, test-tube crypts crowded with goblet cells whose mucus lubricates an increasingly solid stool. Solitary lymphoid follicles are scattered in the mucosa.

Outside, the longitudinal muscle is gathered into three bands, the taeniae coli. Because they are shorter than the tube, the wall bunches into haustra. Fat-filled appendices epiploicae hang from the serosa.
steps.clinical: The three taeniae converge on the base of the appendix — follow a taenia down the caecum at operation and it leads you to the appendix, wherever its tip has wandered.

check.q: Name three features that distinguish colon from small intestine in section.
check.a: No villi; straight crypts with abundant goblet cells; longitudinal muscle concentrated into taeniae coli.

steps.title: Two nerve plexuses
steps.text:
The gut has its own nervous system. The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies in the submucosa and controls secretion, local blood flow and the muscularis mucosae. The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal coats and drives peristalsis.

Both are built from neural crest cells that migrate down the gut in the embryo, cranial to caudal. Parasympathetic fibres (vagus, pelvic splanchnics) and sympathetic fibres modulate them but are not needed for peristalsis to happen.
steps.mnemonic: Meissner is nearer the mucosa (secretion); Auerbach is among the muscle and makes the gut act.
steps.clinical: In Hirschsprung disease neural crest cells fail to reach the distal colon. The aganglionic segment — always including the rectum — cannot relax, and the bowel above it dilates. Achalasia is the same idea at the other end: loss of myenteric neurons at the lower oesophageal sphincter.

check.q: Where is the myenteric plexus, and what does it control?
check.a: Between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa; it controls motility (peristalsis).

title: From the tracheal wall to the alveolus
summary: What changes in the wall on the way down, and why each disease picks the level it does.
objectives: Describe the layers of the tracheal wall and the mucociliary escalator
Explain how the airway wall changes from bronchus to bronchiole to alveolus
Define the acinus and relate it to the two patterns of emphysema
Describe the blood–air barrier and the two types of pneumocyte
takeaways: C-shaped hyaline rings open behind, closed by trachealis; the lining is pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.
Cartilage and glands disappear at the bronchiole; club cells replace goblet cells; smooth muscle persists.
The acinus is everything distal to one terminal bronchiole — the unit of gas exchange.
Type I pneumocytes form the barrier; type II make surfactant and replace type I.
Pulmonary arteries run with the airways; pulmonary veins run in the septa between lobules.

steps.title: The trachea: a tube that must not collapse
steps.text:
About 16–20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage hold the trachea open against the negative pressure of inspiration. The rings are open posteriorly, where the gap is bridged by the trachealis smooth muscle and fibroelastic tissue, next to the oesophagus. Between the rings run anular ligaments of fibrous tissue that let the tube lengthen when you look up.

Inside the cartilage is a submucosa with seromucous glands, then the lamina propria and epithelium.
steps.clinical: Prolonged intubation with an over-inflated cuff can cause pressure necrosis of the mucosa and rings, healing with a tracheal stenosis. Tracheomalacia is the opposite — soft rings that collapse on expiration.

check.q: Why are the tracheal rings open posteriorly?
check.a: So the oesophagus behind can expand when a bolus passes, and so trachealis can narrow the lumen to speed air in a cough.

steps.title: The mucociliary escalator
steps.text:
The airway is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium: every cell touches the basement membrane but not all reach the lumen, so the nuclei sit at different heights. Scattered goblet cells and the submucosal mucous and serous glands make a two-layer film — a watery periciliary layer in which cilia beat, and a sticky mucus blanket on top that traps particles.

The cilia beat in a coordinated wave towards the larynx, clearing the blanket at a few millimetres a minute to be swallowed.
steps.clinical: Smoking paralyses cilia and converts the epithelium to squamous metaplasia, so mucus is cleared only by coughing. Primary ciliary dyskinesia (with situs inversus in Kartagener syndrome) and cystic fibrosis, where the periciliary layer is too dehydrated for the cilia to beat, both end in bronchiectasis.

check.q: What epithelium lines the trachea, and what are its two secretory sources?
check.a: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; goblet cells within it and seromucous glands in the submucosa.

steps.title: Losing the cartilage
steps.text:
In the bronchi the rings break up into irregular cartilage plates, and the smooth muscle forms a continuous spiral inside them. At about 1 mm diameter, the bronchiole, cartilage and glands are gone altogether. The epithelium becomes simple cuboidal, goblet cells give way to club (Clara) cells that secrete surfactant-like protein and detoxify inhaled chemicals, and the wall is mostly smooth muscle.

The last purely conducting segment is the terminal bronchiole, which you can see in the model entering the acinus.
steps.clinical: Because bronchioles depend on surrounding lung for their calibre, they narrow on expiration when that traction falls — and in emphysema, where the alveolar walls are destroyed, they collapse early, trapping air. In asthma it is the bronchiolar smooth muscle that constricts.

check.q: What holds a bronchiole open once it has no cartilage?
check.a: Radial traction from the elastic alveolar walls attached around it — the lung pulls it open.

steps.title: The acinus
steps.text:
An acinus is all the lung supplied by one terminal bronchiole: respiratory bronchioles with alveoli budding from their walls, then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli. It is the unit of gas exchange, a few millimetres across. Several acini make a secondary lobule, outlined by connective tissue septa.

Watch the model's respiratory bronchiole: its wall is interrupted by alveoli — the first place where air meets blood.
steps.clinical: Centriacinar emphysema destroys the respiratory bronchioles in the middle of the acinus, is worst in the upper lobes and is caused by smoking. Panacinar emphysema destroys the whole acinus evenly, is worst in the lower lobes, and is the pattern of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

check.q: Which structure defines the start of an acinus?
check.a: The terminal bronchiole — the acinus is everything distal to it.

steps.title: The blood–air barrier
steps.text:
The alveolar wall is lined almost entirely by type I pneumocytes — flat cells covering about 95% of the surface. Where a capillary presses against the wall, the type I cell, a fused basement membrane and the capillary endothelium are all that separate air from blood: less than a micrometre.

Cuboidal type II pneumocytes sit at the corners. They secrete surfactant from lamellar bodies, lowering surface tension so small alveoli do not collapse, and they divide to replace injured type I cells. Alveolar macrophages roam the surface.
steps.clinical: Surfactant production starts late in gestation, so infants born very prematurely develop respiratory distress syndrome; maternal corticosteroids before delivery speed type II cell maturation. In left heart failure, macrophages that have eaten extravasated red cells fill with haemosiderin — 'heart failure cells'.

check.q: Which cell makes surfactant, and which cell forms most of the gas-exchange surface?
check.a: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant; type I pneumocytes form the barrier.

steps.title: Arteries with the airways, veins in the septa
steps.text:
The pulmonary arteries branch alongside the bronchi and bronchioles, so a pulmonary arteriole sits in the centre of the acinus next to its airway. The pulmonary veins collect blood from the periphery of the acini and run in the interlobular septa, away from the airways, only joining them again near the hilum.

The airway walls themselves are nourished separately, by the bronchial arteries from the aorta.
steps.clinical: This is why interstitial oedema thickens the septa and shows as Kerley B lines on a chest film — the fluid collects where the veins and lymphatics run.

check.q: Where do the pulmonary veins run within a lobule?
check.a: In the interlobular septa at the periphery, not alongside the bronchioles.

title: The nephron, segment by segment
summary: Filter, reclaim, concentrate, fine-tune — and where each diuretic acts.
objectives: Describe the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier
Name the parts of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and what each senses or secretes
Give the main job of each tubular segment and the diuretic that acts there
Explain how the loop and the vasa recta build and keep the medullary gradient
takeaways: Filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms.
Macula densa senses NaCl; juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole release renin.
The proximal tubule reclaims two thirds of the filtrate and all the glucose — and is the segment most easily injured.
Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb; thiazides block NCC in the distal convoluted tubule.
The collecting duct is where aldosterone and ADH set the final sodium and water balance.

steps.title: The renal corpuscle
steps.text:
A tuft of glomerular capillaries hangs between an afferent and an efferent arteriole — arterioles at both ends, so pressure in the tuft stays high enough to filter along its whole length. The tuft is wrapped by the visceral layer of Bowman capsule, the podocytes, whose interdigitating foot processes are bridged by slit diaphragms. The parietal layer lines the outside of the capsule, and the space between drains into the proximal tubule.

Filtrate crosses three layers: fenestrated endothelium, the thick glomerular basement membrane, and the slit diaphragms (nephrin).
steps.clinical: Damage to podocytes (minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis) lets protein through: the nephrotic syndrome of heavy proteinuria and oedema. Inflammation that breaks the capillary wall lets red cells through: the nephritic syndrome of haematuria, hypertension and falling function.

check.q: Name the three layers of the filtration barrier.
check.a: Fenestrated capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and the podocyte slit diaphragms.

steps.title: The juxtaglomerular apparatus
steps.text:
After looping into the medulla, every tubule returns to touch its own glomerulus at the vascular pole. There the wall of the distal tubule is thickened into the macula densa, which senses the NaCl reaching it. Opposite it, modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole — the juxtaglomerular cells — store and release renin.

Low NaCl delivery, low afferent pressure and sympathetic stimulation all release renin, starting the angiotensin–aldosterone cascade.
steps.clinical: In renal artery stenosis the poorly perfused kidney releases renin and drives hypertension. Its filtration depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole, which is why an ACE inhibitor can precipitate acute kidney injury in bilateral stenosis.

check.q: What does the macula densa sense, and what do the juxtaglomerular cells secrete?
check.a: The macula densa senses the NaCl concentration in the distal tubule; juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin.

steps.title: The proximal tubule: the bulk reclaimer
steps.text:
The proximal convoluted tubule has tall cells with a dense brush border and packed mitochondria. It reabsorbs about two thirds of filtered sodium and water, all the filtered glucose and amino acids, most of the bicarbonate and phosphate — and it secretes organic acids and many drugs.

It then straightens and dives towards the medulla as the straight proximal tubule.
steps.clinical: All that active transport makes the proximal tubule — especially its straight part in the outer medulla — the most vulnerable to ischaemia and to toxins such as aminoglycosides and contrast: acute tubular necrosis. SGLT2 inhibitors act here, causing glycosuria.

check.q: Which tubular segment reabsorbs all filtered glucose?
check.a: The proximal convoluted tubule (via SGLT2 and SGLT1).

steps.title: The loop of Henle and the vasa recta
steps.text:
The thin descending limb is permeable to water but not salt; the thick ascending limb is impermeable to water and pumps salt out through the Na–K–2Cl co-transporter (NKCC2). Running in opposite directions side by side, they multiply a small difference into a gradient from about 300 mOsm/kg in the cortex to about 1200 at the papilla — the countercurrent multiplier.

The vasa recta, hairpin capillaries from juxtamedullary efferent arterioles, follow the same loops. As countercurrent exchangers they supply the medulla without washing the gradient away.
steps.mnemonic: The thick ascending limb is the diluting segment: salt out, water stays in — so fluid leaving it is always hypotonic.

check.q: Which transporter do loop diuretics block, and where is it?
check.a: NKCC2, in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

steps.title: Distal tubule and collecting duct: the fine tuning
steps.text:
The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs a further 5–10% of sodium through the Na–Cl co-transporter, the target of thiazides, and is where calcium reabsorption is regulated by PTH.

The collecting duct decides the final urine. Principal cells take up sodium through ENaC channels under aldosterone and insert aquaporin-2 water channels under ADH, letting water leave into the hypertonic medulla. Intercalated cells secrete acid or bicarbonate.
steps.clinical: Amiloride blocks ENaC and spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor — both potassium-sparing because they reduce the sodium entry that drives potassium secretion. Lithium damages principal cells and is a classic cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

check.q: Which hormone inserts water channels in the collecting duct, and what happens without it?
check.a: ADH (vasopressin) inserts aquaporin-2; without it, or if the duct cannot respond, large volumes of dilute urine are passed — diabetes insipidus.

steps.title: The bladder wall: a lining that stretches
steps.text:
Urine leaves through a tube lined by urothelium from the renal pelvis to the proximal urethra. Its surface umbrella cells are large, often binucleate, and their apical membrane carries rigid uroplakin plaques that fold away when the bladder is empty and unfold as it fills — an impermeable barrier against hypertonic urine.

Beneath is a lamina propria and the detrusor: three interlacing layers of smooth muscle that contract together, under pelvic splanchnic (S2–4) parasympathetic control, to empty the bladder.
steps.clinical: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma can arise anywhere the urothelium goes, and often in several places at once — so painless haematuria needs imaging of the upper tract as well as cystoscopy. Smoking and aromatic amines are the main risk factors.

check.q: Why does the urothelium not become leaky as the bladder stretches?
check.a: Its umbrella cells flatten and unfold stored membrane plaques instead of separating; tight junctions and uroplakins keep it impermeable.

title: Muscle, nerve and bone under the microscope
summary: Three tissues wrapped in the same way — and what that wrapping means for injury and repair.
objectives: Name the connective tissue sheaths of a skeletal muscle and a peripheral nerve
Describe the neuromuscular junction and the muscle spindle
Contrast skeletal and cardiac muscle and explain why the heart heals by scar
Grade a peripheral nerve injury by which layers are cut
Describe an osteon and the role of the periosteum in fracture healing
takeaways: Muscle: epimysium, perimysium, endomysium. Nerve: epineurium, perineurium, endoneurium.
The perineurium is the blood–nerve barrier; the endoneurial tube is the regenerating axon's guide.
Neurapraxia recovers fully; axonotmesis regrows at about 1 mm a day; neurotmesis needs repair.
Cardiac muscle cells are branched, joined by intercalated discs, and cannot divide.
The osteon is a cylinder of lamellae round a Haversian canal; the periosteum's cambium layer makes callus.

steps.title: Three sheaths round a muscle
steps.text:
A skeletal muscle is wrapped in epimysium, a dense collagen coat continuous with the tendon. Septa of perimysium divide it into fascicles, the bundles you can see in a steak, and carry the larger vessels and nerves. Each fibre inside a fascicle has its own delicate endomysium, holding the capillaries.

A muscle fibre is a single huge cell formed by fusion of myoblasts: many nuclei pushed to the periphery, the rest filled with myofibrils whose sarcomeres give the striations.
steps.clinical: Satellite cells beneath the basal lamina of each fibre let skeletal muscle regenerate after injury — provided the endomysial scaffold survives. In compartment syndrome the fibres die of ischaemia and are replaced by scar, leaving a contracture.

check.q: Which sheath surrounds a fascicle?
check.a: The perimysium.

steps.title: Motor end plate and muscle spindle
steps.text:
A motor nerve branch enters with the vessels and divides so that each fibre gets a single neuromuscular junction. One motor neuron and all the fibres it supplies form a motor unit — a few fibres in the eye muscles, a thousand or more in gluteus maximus.

The muscle spindle is a capsule holding a few thin intrafusal fibres lying parallel to the ordinary fibres. It reports stretch through Ia afferents; gamma motor neurons tighten it so it stays sensitive as the muscle shortens. It is the receptor of every tendon reflex.
steps.clinical: In myasthenia gravis antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor at the junction cause fatigable weakness, worst in the small motor units of the eyelids and eyes — hence ptosis and diplopia first.

check.q: What receptor is stimulated when you tap the patellar tendon?
check.a: The muscle spindles of quadriceps, which are stretched and fire Ia afferents to the cord.

steps.title: Cardiac muscle: a branching network
steps.text:
Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but its cells are short, branched and have one or two central nuclei. They join end to end at intercalated discs: desmosomes and adherens junctions hold them together under load, and gap junctions let the action potential pass from cell to cell, so the myocardium contracts as a functional syncytium.

The cells are packed with mitochondria and fed by a very dense capillary bed — the heart takes most of the oxygen from its coronary blood even at rest.
steps.clinical: The scar does not conduct or contract: it causes regional wall-motion loss, can bulge into an aneurysm, and its border is a common source of re-entrant ventricular tachycardia.

check.q: Why does an infarcted area of myocardium heal with scar instead of new muscle?
check.a: Adult cardiomyocytes essentially cannot divide and the heart has no satellite-cell equivalent, so dead muscle is replaced by fibrous tissue.

steps.title: Three sheaths round a nerve
steps.text:
A peripheral nerve repeats the muscle's plan. Epineurium — dense collagen with fat and vasa nervorum — wraps the whole nerve. Each fascicle is surrounded by perineurium, layers of flattened cells joined by tight junctions: the blood–nerve barrier. Each axon lies in delicate endoneurium.

Large axons are myelinated by Schwann cells, one cell per internode, with nodes of Ranvier between them for saltatory conduction. Small pain and autonomic C fibres are unmyelinated, several tucked into one Remak Schwann cell.
steps.clinical: Diabetes damages the vasa nervorum and the longest axons first, giving a length-dependent 'glove and stocking' neuropathy that starts in the toes.

check.q: Which layer of a peripheral nerve forms the diffusion barrier?
check.a: The perineurium, whose cells are joined by tight junctions.

steps.title: Grading a nerve injury
steps.text:
Neurapraxia: a local conduction block, usually demyelination from compression; the axon is intact and recovery is complete in weeks. Axonotmesis: the axon is cut but the endoneurial tubes survive. The distal axon undergoes Wallerian degeneration, and the stump regrows down its own tube at about 1 mm a day, to the right target. Neurotmesis: the whole nerve is divided; without surgical repair axons sprout into scar and form a neuroma.

This is the Seddon classification, and the sheaths are its logic.
steps.clinical: An advancing Tinel sign — tingling on tapping over the regenerating tip, moving distally week by week — is the bedside sign that regrowth is under way.

check.q: After axonotmesis of the radial nerve 200 mm above its first reinnervated muscle, how long before recovery might begin?
check.a: About 200 days — axons regrow roughly 1 mm a day down the intact endoneurial tubes.

steps.title: Compact bone and the periosteum
steps.text:
Cortical bone is built of osteons: cylinders of concentric lamellae around a Haversian canal carrying vessels and nerves, running along the long axis. Osteocytes sit in lacunae between the lamellae and touch each other through canaliculi. Transverse Volkmann canals link the Haversian canals with each other and with the surfaces. Fragments of old osteons, cut through by remodelling, remain as interstitial lamellae, bounded by cement lines.

Outside is the periosteum: a fibrous layer anchored by Sharpey fibres, and an inner cambium layer of osteoprogenitor cells.
steps.clinical: Periosteum is richly innervated — the reason a fracture or a periosteal tumour hurts so much — and a child's thick, loosely attached periosteum lets greenstick fractures heal fast and remodel well.

check.q: Which layer of the periosteum forms fracture callus?
check.a: The inner cambium (osteogenic) layer, whose osteoprogenitor cells multiply and lay down new bone.

title: The cornea and the retina in 3D
summary: The clearest tissue in the body and the most layered one — and what each layer does when it fails.
objectives: Name the five layers of the cornea and explain its transparency
Trace light and signal through the layers of the retina
Explain what separates in a retinal detachment and why
Relate the fovea and the dual blood supply to macular disease and arterial occlusion
takeaways: Cornea: epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Descemet membrane, endothelium.
Corneal transparency depends on regular collagen lamellae and a pumping endothelium that cannot regenerate.
Light crosses the inner retina to reach the photoreceptors; signals return via bipolar to ganglion cells.
Detachment splits the neural retina from the pigment epithelium — the old optic-vesicle cleft.
The inner retina is fed by the central retinal artery, the outer retina by the choriocapillaris.

steps.title: Five layers of the cornea
steps.text:
From the front: a stratified squamous epithelium five or six cells thick, kept wet by the tear film; the acellular Bowman layer; the stroma, nine tenths of the thickness; Descemet membrane, the thick basement membrane of the last layer; and the single-layer endothelium.

The stroma is transparent because its collagen fibrils are all the same diameter and evenly spaced, in lamellae that cross at angles, with flattened keratocytes between them. The cornea has no blood vessels at all — it takes oxygen from the air and nutrients from the aqueous.

check.q: Name the five layers of the cornea, front to back.
check.a: Epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Descemet membrane, endothelium.

steps.title: Why the cornea heals — and why it clouds
steps.text:
The corneal epithelium regenerates quickly from limbal stem cells at the corneal edge: an abrasion is covered within a day or two. The endothelium cannot divide. It pumps water out of the stroma constantly; as cells are lost with age, surgery or disease, the survivors spread to cover the gap, until too few remain and the stroma swells and clouds.

The epithelium is densely innervated by the long ciliary nerves (V1) — the reason an abrasion is so painful, and the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.
steps.clinical: Fuchs endothelial dystrophy produces morning blurring from stromal oedema and is a leading reason for corneal transplantation. The corneal reflex tests V1 (afferent) and VII (efferent), and a unilateral loss is an early sign of a cerebellopontine angle tumour.

check.q: Why does a corneal abrasion heal in a day, while endothelial loss is permanent?
check.a: The epithelium regenerates from limbal stem cells; adult corneal endothelial cells cannot divide, they only spread.

steps.title: Light goes in, the signal comes back
steps.text:
The retina is inside out. Light passes through the nerve fibre layer, ganglion cells, inner plexiform, inner nuclear and outer plexiform layers before reaching the rods and cones, whose nuclei make the outer nuclear layer. The signal then travels back: photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell, with horizontal and amacrine cells shaping it sideways.

Ganglion cell axons run across the inner surface to the optic disc and become the optic nerve. Müller glia span the whole thickness as scaffolding.
steps.pitfall: The 'outer' and 'inner' in the layer names are relative to the centre of the eye: the outer nuclear layer (photoreceptors) is the one nearest the choroid.

check.q: Whose axons form the optic nerve?
check.a: The retinal ganglion cells'.

steps.title: The pigment epithelium and the detachment plane
steps.text:
Behind the photoreceptors lies the retinal pigment epithelium, a single layer of cells that absorbs stray light, recycles visual pigment and phagocytoses the tips of the outer segments every day. Behind it are Bruch membrane, the choriocapillaris and the choroid.

The neural retina and the RPE develop from the two layers of the optic cup, and the potential space between them — the old cavity of the optic vesicle — is never sealed. It is the plane that opens in a retinal detachment.
steps.clinical: Detached photoreceptors lose their supply from the choriocapillaris and begin to die within days — flashes, floaters and a curtain across the field are an emergency. Central retinal artery occlusion, by contrast, infarcts the inner retina, which whitens around a fovea that stays red because it has no inner layers: the cherry-red spot.

check.q: In a retinal detachment, which two layers separate?
check.a: The neural retina (photoreceptor layer) separates from the retinal pigment epithelium.

steps.title: Rods, cones and the fovea
steps.text:
About 120 million rods work in dim light and see no colour; about 6 million cones work in bright light and see colour and fine detail. Cones are concentrated at the fovea, a pit in the centre of the macula where the inner layers are pushed aside, there are no rods and no retinal vessels, and each cone has a nearly private line to a ganglion cell.

The fovea is served entirely by the choroid — the most metabolically demanding patch of retina with no retinal circulation of its own.
steps.clinical: Age-related macular degeneration begins with drusen — deposits in Bruch membrane beneath the RPE — and in its wet form new choroidal vessels break through Bruch membrane and bleed under the macula. Central vision is lost while peripheral vision is spared.

check.q: Why is visual acuity highest at the fovea?
check.a: Cones are densest there, inner layers and vessels are displaced so light reaches them undistorted, and there is little convergence onto ganglion cells.

title: Endocrine tissue under the microscope
summary: Follicles, islets and zones: how the build of each gland tells you what it makes.
objectives: Describe the thyroid follicle and the steps of thyroid hormone synthesis
Identify the parafollicular C cells and their tumour
Describe the endocrine and exocrine pancreas and the cell types of the islet
Name the zones of the adrenal cortex, their products and the adrenal blood flow
takeaways: The thyroid stores its hormone outside the cells, as thyroglobulin in colloid.
Tall follicular cells and scalloped colloid mean an active gland; flat cells and full colloid a resting one.
C cells make calcitonin and give rise to medullary carcinoma.
Islets are 1–2% of the pancreas: beta (insulin) in the centre, alpha (glucagon) and delta (somatostatin) around.
Adrenal cortex: glomerulosa (salt), fasciculata (sugar), reticularis (sex) — blood flows through them to the medulla.

steps.title: The thyroid follicle
steps.text:
The thyroid is made of spherical follicles, each a single layer of follicular cells around a lumen of colloid — stored thyroglobulin. It is the only endocrine gland that stores its product outside the cells, enough for several weeks.

The height of the epithelium tells you how hard it is working: flat cells with a lumen full of colloid in a resting gland, tall columnar cells with pale, scalloped colloid in an over-stimulated one. Dense perifollicular capillaries with fenestrated endothelium surround every follicle.

check.q: What does the height of the follicular epithelium tell you?
check.a: Its activity: tall cells with scant colloid indicate stimulation (for example Graves disease); flat cells with abundant colloid indicate a resting gland.

steps.title: Making thyroid hormone
steps.text:
The follicular cell traps iodide from blood (the sodium–iodide symporter), passes it to the apical surface, and there thyroid peroxidase oxidises it and attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin in the colloid, coupling them into T4 and T3. Under TSH the cell engulfs colloid, digests the thyroglobulin in lysosomes and releases T4 and T3 at its base.

Between the follicles sit pale parafollicular C cells, derived from the ultimobranchial body of the fourth pouch, which secrete calcitonin.
steps.clinical: Radioactive iodine is taken up through the same symporter, which is how it treats Graves disease and differentiated thyroid cancer. Medullary carcinoma does not take up iodine; calcitonin is its tumour marker.

check.q: Which cells make calcitonin, and which tumour arises from them?
check.a: The parafollicular C cells; medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (sporadic or in MEN 2).

steps.title: The parathyroids
steps.text:
Behind the thyroid lie four small parathyroid glands. They are packed sheets of chief cells, which secrete parathyroid hormone in response to a fall in ionised calcium, with larger pink oxyphil cells that increase with age, and fat that increases too.

PTH raises blood calcium by releasing it from bone, increasing its reabsorption in the distal tubule and stimulating renal activation of vitamin D.
steps.clinical: Accidental removal or devascularisation of the parathyroids during thyroidectomy causes hypocalcaemia within days — perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs. A single adenoma is the usual cause of primary hyperparathyroidism.

check.q: Which parathyroid cell secretes PTH?
check.a: The chief cell.

steps.title: Two glands in the pancreas
steps.text:
Most of the pancreas is exocrine: serous acini of pyramidal cells with basophilic bases and apical zymogen granules, draining through intercalated ducts (whose centroacinar cells add bicarbonate) into the duct system.

Scattered among them are the pale islets of Langerhans, about a million, 1–2% of the mass. Beta cells (insulin, about 70%) fill the centre; alpha cells (glucagon), delta cells (somatostatin) and PP cells sit mainly at the periphery. Islet blood flows on to the acini around them, bathing them in high insulin.
steps.clinical: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of beta cells, leaving the other islet cells intact. In chronic pancreatitis the acini are lost first; the islets survive longer, but diabetes eventually follows as they are strangled by fibrosis.

check.q: Which islet cell is most numerous, and what does it secrete?
check.a: The beta cell; insulin.

steps.title: The adrenal: salt, sugar, sex
steps.text:
The adrenal cortex has three zones. Beneath the capsule, the zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone under angiotensin II and potassium. The broad zona fasciculata, columns of pale lipid-laden cells, makes cortisol under ACTH. The zona reticularis makes adrenal androgens.

Blood runs from capsular arteries through sinusoids in the cortex into the medulla, whose chromaffin cells secrete adrenaline and noradrenaline. The high cortisol in that blood induces the enzyme (PNMT) that converts noradrenaline to adrenaline.
steps.mnemonic: GFR from outside in, making salt, sugar, sex — and the deeper you go, the sweeter it gets.
steps.clinical: A phaeochromocytoma arises from medullary chromaffin cells and causes episodic hypertension, headache and sweating; a zona glomerulosa adenoma causes Conn syndrome — hypertension with hypokalaemia.

check.q: Name the three cortical zones from outside in, with the main product of each.
check.a: Glomerulosa — aldosterone; fasciculata — cortisol; reticularis — androgens.
